name: Go goroutines (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (goroutine versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Go (go1.8.1): 0.42-0.49 us per goroutine (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 110x-175x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Go side: go1.8.1, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: Goroutines run on the Go runtime's user-space scheduler with a garbage-collected heap and growable stacks; the cost is runtime size, GC pauses and no manual control of placement. Calling C from Go (cgo) is slower than a C call.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it.
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; opened the .qbk source on github.com and the skynet repo.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: goroutines are user-space units scheduled by the Go runtime, while pthreads are OS threads (the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources). No explicit mechanism is given.

name: Erlang/OTP processes (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (Erlang process versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Erlang (erts-8.3): 0.63-0.73 us per process (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 74x-116x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Erlang side: erts-8.3, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: BEAM processes have private heaps and communicate by copying messages; per-process GC, no shared mutable state, and a VM that is slower than C for numeric code.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. In the upstream skynet README the Erlang run needs erl +P 2000000 to raise the process limit; that option is not mentioned on the Boost.Fiber page.
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Erlang row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: Erlang processes are lightweight units scheduled by the BEAM, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

name: .NET Regex compiled mode (dotnet/compiled) in rebar vs PCRE2 JIT and RE2
baseline: PCRE2 10.47 with JIT (C) and RE2 2025-11-05 (C++), as measured by rebar
workload: rebar curated regex search benchmarks (34 benchmarks measured for dotnet/compiled: literal, literal-alternate, aws-keys, words, cloudflare ReDoS, Unicode and others) with the regex engines driven from per-engine runner programs.
claimed_speedup: Search-time geometric mean of speed ratios (lower is better): hyperscan 2.37, rust/regex 3.08, dotnet/compiled 3.60, pcre2/jit 6.00, dotnet/nobacktrack 6.36, re2 10.39, java/hotspot 42.24. Per benchmark: literal/sherlock-zh dotnet/compiled 48.0 GB/s vs pcre2/jit 41.7 GB/s and hyperscan 45.0 GB/s; literal-alternate/sherlock-zh 27.4 GB/s vs hyperscan 19.8 GB/s and pcre2/jit 2.6 GB/s; cloud-flare-redos/simplified-short 95.0 GB/s vs hyperscan 82.4 MB/s. Compile time is worse: geometric mean 19.79 for dotnet/compiled vs 6.20 for pcre2/jit and 12.28 for re2.
compiler_and_flags: .NET 10.0.0 (RegexOptions.Compiled via the dotnet runner); PCRE2 and RE2 are vendored and built by rebar (build flags not read)
stars_or_usage: dotnet/runtime 18.3k stars; rebar 326 stars (rebar README results recorded 2025-12-19, rebar last commit 2026-06-28)
tradeoffs: Regex matches UTF-16 code units, not code points (rebar notes \w and . miss non-BMP code points); Unicode mode cannot be turned off; much slower to compile patterns than PCRE2 (compile-time geometric mean 19.79 vs 1.41 for pcre2 interpreter); invalid UTF-8 haystacks throw.
caveats: Independent suite (rebar, by the author of Rust regex, who states the barometer is biased toward Rust regex) with public benchmark code and engine versions, but the README does not state the CPU, so capped at B. Engines differ in algorithm and semantics (backtracking with vectorized prefix search, Unicode-aware classes), and rebar notes dotnet/compiled gets a different match count on some benchmarks. The 95.0 GB/s ReDoS row looks like an early-exit effect rather than scanning. Java (java/hotspot) is far behind (geometric mean 42.24), so the finding applies to .NET only. Reported as evidence for the known dotnet/runtime entry (System.Text.RegularExpressions). Geometric means are over different benchmark subsets per engine (34 for dotnet/compiled and pcre2/jit, 31 for re2). The rebar README page was read only to its first 100,000 characters via WebFetch plus the full raw README by curl.
found_via: WebSearch for '.NET C# faster than C++ benchmark ...' returned only blog posts; opened github.com/BurntSushi/rebar (README summary tables) while checking regex shootouts for managed runtimes.
why_faster: dotnet/compiled is RegexOptions.Compiled: the pattern is compiled to IL and JIT-compiled at run time (rebar engines/dotnet README); the rebar page does not explain the individual per-benchmark wins.

name: hyper (HttpArena h2 and pipelined rows vs C and C++ servers)
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG); h2o (C), proxygen and Drogon and agensio (C++) rows in the same suite
workload: HttpArena baseline-h2 (HTTP/2 over TLS, 256 and 1024 connections), 16x pipelined HTTP/1.1, baseline-4096 and limited-conn profiles for the HttpArena hyper entry (hyper 1 with hyper-util, multi-threaded tokio runtime, rustls).
claimed_speedup: baseline-h2-256: 6,974,787 req/s vs nginx 3,414,750 (2.04x, derived from page data), proxygen (C++) 5,845,844 (1.19x), but h2o 16,106,978 (0.43x) and agensio 14,744,015 (0.47x) are far ahead. baseline-h2-1024: 5,157,286 vs nginx 3,320,285 (1.55x). pipelined-4096: 16,218,012 vs nginx 4,037,345 (4.0x), Drogon 7,801,404 (2.08x), libreactorng 43,424,448 (0.37x). Slower than nginx on plain HTTP/1.1: baseline-4096 3,003,360 vs 3,284,513 (0.91x), limited-conn-4096 2,362,875 vs 2,626,297 (0.90x); static-h2-256 407,071 vs 802,090 (0.51x).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.94 (rust:1.94 image), RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release with opt-level 3, lto=true, codegen-units 1 (frameworks/hyper/Cargo.toml and Dockerfile). C/C++ baseline flags as in the zix record.
hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine per site/data/current.json: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX 64-Cores (64 cores, 128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), CPU governor performance; each entry runs in a container. current.json is undated and may differ from the machine state of the run behind a given results file.
tradeoffs: Low-level library; the HttpArena entry is a hand-written minimal handler on hyper-util with a work-stealing multi-thread tokio runtime.
caveats: Evidence for the already-listed hyper entry using a C and C++ baseline instead of actix-web. Mixed: hyper beats nginx on HTTP/2 baseline and pipelined profiles, loses to h2o and agensio on HTTP/2, and is slower than nginx, libreactorng, libioma and mongoose on plain HTTP/1.1. Response size is 112.5 bytes at baseline-4096 versus 135.4 for nginx. HttpArena results JSON files are undated, hold one 5 s run per profile with no repeat count stated, and are rerun by the maintainers, so the numbers can move. The C competitor entries (nginx with a custom C handler module, libreactorng, libioma, h2o, mongoose) are minimal hand-written handlers built by the suite maintainers or contributors, not tuned production configurations; the C/C++ rows are compiled with -O3 -march=native (nginx, libreactorng, libioma, mongoose; libioma and mongoose also with LTO) or CMake Release with clang -march=native (h2o), and the Drogon entry compiles only its handler with CMake Release against the prebuilt drogonframework/drogon:latest Docker image (the Drogon library's own flags are not under the suite's control, so Drogon ratios of 2x to 8x here are weaker evidence than the nginx, h2o, libreactorng and libioma ratios). Response sizes differ between entries (bytes per response derived from bandwidth divided by req/s in the same JSON files: nginx 135.4, Drogon 134.4, libreactorng 108.7, libioma 85.8, mongoose 72.5, versus 62.9 for the Zig, Rust and C# entries at baseline-4096), so the minimal-header entries write fewer bytes per request. The pipelined profile (16x batched pipelining) is reference-only in HttpArena's own composite score.
found_via: HttpArena site/data/results/hyper.json compared with nginx.json, h2o.json, agensio.json and proxygen.json via raw.githubusercontent.com; frameworks/hyper Cargo.toml and Dockerfile opened
why_faster: hyper's HTTP/2 implementation with one tokio multi-thread runtime versus nginx's HTTP/2 path in this suite; no explicit mechanism stated by the suite.
